title: Self-Trapping and Liouvillian Spectral Transitions in a Dissipative Bose-Hubbard Dimer
abstract: We study the self-trapping transition in dissipative double wells using mean-field theory and exact diagonalization. We find that, similar to the conventional interaction-driven transition from oscillatory dynamics to self-trapping, dissipation alone can also induce self-trapping-like localization in one well. The resulting state, although transient and decaying, persists for a substantial time. At the mean-field level, the interaction- and dissipation-driven transitions are discontinuous and continuous, respectively. When interaction and dissipation both are present, their interplay produces three dynamical regimes: (i) at weak interaction, increasing dissipation drives a transition from oscillations to self-trapping; (ii) at moderate interaction, self-trapping at weak dissipation, oscillatory dynamics at intermediate dissipation, and re-entrant self-trapping at strong dissipation; and (iii) at strong interaction, self-trapping persists but is weakened by dissipation. We connect the transition with the Liouvillian spectrum. It is observed that purely dissipation-driven transition coincides with an exceptional point in the spectra, and a peak in the Liouvillian gap, marking the onset of the quantum-Zeno regime. In the presence of interactions, however, the onset of the Zeno regime is shifted to dissipation strengths larger than that required for the self-trapping transition.
summary: This paper analyzes the self-trapping transition in a dissipative Bose-Hubbard dimer, showing that environmental dissipation can induce localization similar to interaction effects. By analyzing the Liouvillian spectrum, the authors map out complex dynamical regimes resulting from the interplay between interaction and dissipation. The findings provide a detailed spectral understanding of how non-Hermitian effects govern quantum coherence in open quantum systems.
main_problem: The study investigates the self-trapping transition in a dissipative Bose-Hubbard dimer, comparing the effects of interaction versus dissipation on localization.
main_result: Dissipation alone can induce a transient self-trapping-like localization, and the interplay between interaction and dissipation creates complex, multi-regime dynamics.
method: The analysis employs Mean-Field theory and Exact Diagonalization, characterizing the dynamics using the Liouvillian superoperator spectrum.
model_or_system: The system is a Bose-Josephson junction (BJJ) modeled by a Hamiltonian and subjected to dissipation via a Lindblad Master Equation. The model involves tunneling ($J$), on-site interaction ($U$), and a dissipation rate ($\Gamma$).
key_observables: Self-trapping transition, Liouvillian spectrum (eigenvalues), Liouvillian gap, and population imbalance ($z$).
important_parameters: Tunneling rate ($J$), interaction strength ($U$), and dissipation coefficient ($\Gamma$ or $\gamma$).
main_assumptions: The Mean-Field analysis assumes $U$ is an effective nonlinear interaction scale, and the dynamics are governed by the Lindblad Master Equation framework.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the time evolution of population imbalance ($z(t)$) and particle number ($n(t)$) under varying interaction and dissipation strengths, and show the Liouvillian spectrum's dependence on dissipation.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the model using the Hamiltonian and Lindblad equation, then analyzes the transition mechanisms (interaction-driven vs. dissipation-driven) using MF and ED, and finally connects these dynamical transitions to spectral features like exceptional points and the quantum-Zeno regime.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it tackles non-equilibrium dynamics in bosonic systems, using advanced spectral tools (Liouvillian analysis) to characterize phase transitions induced by environmental coupling, a core topic in open quantum systems.

FIG. 2: Plots of population imbalance z(t) for interaction and dissipation-driven dynamics, respectively. (a) MF results varying U at γ = 0 (b) MF results varying γ at U = 0, (c) ED results varying U at γ = 0 for N = 5 (d) ED results varying γ at U = 0 for N = 4
FIG. 3: Plots of time evolution of the normalized particle number n(t). Panels (a)-(b) shows MF method and (c)-(d) shows ED method.

FIG. 5: Dissipation-driven crossover between oscillatory and self-trapped dynamics. (a) Order parameter |⟨z⟩| as a function of γ for different U values. (b) Phase diagram in the U −γ parameter plane, showing the oscillatory and self-trapped dynamical regimes. The color scale represents |⟨z⟩|, with larger values indicating stronger self-trapping.

FIG. 4: Plots of order parameter |⟨z⟩| and susceptibility χ as functions of the interaction strength U and dissipation rate γ. Panels (a) and (c) show the results as U is varied at γ = 0, while (b) and (d) correspond to varying γ at U = 0. Here J = 1, N = 1 were used throughout.
